hints: Look closely at the hydroxide product, as solubility is a great clue to tell Group 1 and Group 2 hydroxides apart.
Recall that $\text{NaOH}$ is very soluble while $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ is only slightly soluble, so this tells you whether Y is Na or Mg.
Work out what hydride Q must be to burn to an oxide where Z is +5, and check whether $\text{PH}_3$ or $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ can do this.
walkthrough:
**Use hydroxide solubility to find Y**

Think like a detective. Group 1 hydroxides like $\text{NaOH}$ dissolve very easily in water.

Group 2 hydroxides like $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ are only slightly soluble (sparingly soluble). Since X gives a slightly soluble hydroxide, Y must be magnesium.

**Identify compound Q as a hydride**

X contains only Y and Z, and reacts with water to give $\text{Y-OH}$ plus Q.

Q contains only Z and hydrogen, so Q must be a hydride of Z:
$$\text{Mg}_3\text{Z}_x + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Mg(OH)}_2 + \text{H}_m\text{Z}$$

**Use the burning reaction to find Z**

Q burns to give an oxide of Z where Z has oxidation number +5 plus water. Test the two possibilities.

If $\text{Z = P}$, then $\text{Q = PH}_3$ which burns to $\text{P}_2\text{O}_5$ where P is +5. If $\text{Z = S}$, then $\text{Q = H}_2\text{S}$ which burns to $\text{SO}_2$ where S is +4, not +5. So Z must be phosphorus.

**Put it together**

Y is Mg and Z is P. This fits magnesium phosphide:
$$\text{Mg}_3\text{P}_2 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 3\text{Mg(OH)}_2 + 2\text{PH}_3$$

options.A: Correct. Y = Mg gives slightly soluble $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$. Z = P gives $\text{Q = PH}_3$ which burns in air to a P(V) oxide such as $\text{P}_2\text{O}_5$ where P is +5. This matches all three clues.
options.B: Incorrect. Y = Na would give $\text{NaOH}$ which is highly soluble, not slightly soluble. Also Z = S would give $\text{Q = H}_2\text{S}$ which burns to $\text{SO}_2$ where S is +4, not +5.
options.C: Incorrect. Although Z = P correctly gives $\text{PH}_3$ burning to a P(+5) oxide, Y = Na is wrong because $\text{NaOH}$ is very soluble in water, not slightly soluble.
options.D: Incorrect. Y = Mg correctly gives slightly soluble $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$, but Z = S is wrong because $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ burns to $\text{SO}_2$ or $\text{SO}_3$ chemistry where the common combustion oxide has S at +4, not +5.
